chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-1.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-1.body:
Let $B$ = at least one child born on Tuesday: $P(B)=1-\left(\frac67\right)^2=\frac{13}{49}$. Let $A$ = the first child born on Tuesday: $A\subseteq B$ and $P(A)=\frac17=\frac7{49}$. Hence $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{7/49}{13/49}=\frac7{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{13}$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3b.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3b.body: $P(A)=\frac13$, $P(B)=\frac16$, but $P(A\cap B)=0$ (no multiple of $12$ on a die) $\ne\frac1{18}$. Not independent.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3d.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3d.body: Day $n$ has weekday $n\bmod7$ and day-of-month $n\bmod31$. Since $\gcd(7,31)=1$, by the Chinese Remainder Theorem each of the $7\cdot31$ pairs (weekday, day of month) occurs equally often (once per $217$ days). So $P(A)=\frac17$, $P(B)=\frac1{31}$, $P(A\cap B)=\frac1{217}=P(A)P(B)$. Independent.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3e.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3e.body: $P(A)=P(B)=\frac12$ but $A\cap B$ is the single permutation $321$: $P(A\cap B)=\frac16\ne\frac14$. Not independent.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3f.title: Solution
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3f.body: $B$ happens iff the first flip is H (an initial run of H's ends with the first HT, before any TH; similarly if the first flip is T then TH comes first): $P(B)=\frac12$. For $A$, let $h$ ($t$) be the probability that HH comes before TT given the last flip so far is H (T): $h=\frac12+\frac12t$, $t=\frac12h$, so $h=\frac23$, $t=\frac13$ and $P(A)=\frac12\cdot\frac23+\frac12\cdot\frac13=\frac12$. But $P(A\cap B)=P(\text{first flip H})\cdot h=\frac12\cdot\frac23=\frac13\ne\frac14$. Not independent.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-5.title: Recursion
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-5.body: Let $E$ be the expectation. The first flip is a head with probability $\frac1n$ (stop after $1$ flip); otherwise we are back at the start after one wasted flip: $E=1+\left(1-\frac1n\right)E$, so $\frac En=1$, $E=n$. (Equivalently the number of flips is geometric with mean $n$.) ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-6.title: Continuous
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-6.body: The conditional density is $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}=f_X(x)$, so $E[X\mid Y=y]=\int xf_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)dx=\int xf_X(x)dx=E[X]$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-7.title: Hölder
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-7.body:
(1) With probabilities $P_i$: $E[X]\le E|X|=\sum_i|x_i|P_i=\sum_i\big(|x_i|\sqrt{P_i}\big)\big(\sqrt{P_i}\big)\le\Big(\sum x_i^2P_i\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum P_i\Big)^{1/2}=\sqrt{E[X^2]}$.

(2) $E[X]\le\int|x|f(x)dx=\int\big(|x|\sqrt{f}\big)\sqrt f\,dx\le\Big(\int x^2f\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\int f\Big)^{1/2}=\sqrt{E[X^2]}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-8.title: Continuous
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-8.body: $E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]=\int f_Y(y)\int x\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}dx\,dy=\int x\left(\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)dy\right)dx=\int xf_X(x)dx=E[X]$, where the order of integration is swapped by Fubini's theorem. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-10.title: Induction
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-10.body: By the tower rule, $E[X_n]=E\big[E[X_n\mid X_{n-1},\dots,X_1]\big]=E[X_{n-1}]$, so $E[X_n]=E[X_{n-1}]=\dots=E[X_1]$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-11.title: Check the two martingale conditions
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-11.body:
*Integrability:* $|X'_n|\le|X_1|+\dots+|X_n|$, so $E|X'_n|<\infty$.

*Martingale property:* the event $\{k\le n-1\}$ is determined by $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}$ (equivalently by $X'_1,\dots,X'_{n-1}$). On it, $X'_n=X'_{n-1}$, so the conditional expectation of $X'_n$ is $X'_{n-1}$. On the complementary event $\{k\ge n\}$, $X'_n=X_n$ and $X'_j=X_j$ for $j\le n-1$, so $E[X'_n\mid X'_1,\dots,X'_{n-1}]=E[X_n\mid X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}]=X_{n-1}=X'_{n-1}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-14.title: Example
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-14.body: Let $X_1=0$ and $X_{n+1}=X_n\pm1$ with probability $\frac12$ each (a martingale). Stop at the first $n$ with $X_n=1$. Then $k<\infty$ with probability $1$: starting from $0$, the probability of hitting $1$ before $-N$ is $\frac N{N+1}\to1$ as $N\to\infty$ (gambler's ruin, see the next problems). But $x_k=1$ always, so $E[x_k]=1\ne0=E[x_1]$. The optional stopping conditions fail: $k$ is not bounded, $E[k]=\infty$, and the stopped walk is not bounded below. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-15.title: Martingale
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-15.body:
The position $X_n$ is a martingale and the stopped process is bounded (values in $[0,100]$), so optional stopping gives $E[X_k]=X_1=67$. With $p$ the probability of ending at $100$: $100p+0(1-p)=67$, so $p=\frac{67}{100}$.

**Answer: $\frac{67}{100}$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-16.title: Martingale $X_n^2-n$
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-16.body:
$M_n=X_n^2-n$ is a martingale: $E[X_{n+1}^2\mid X_n]=\frac12(X_n+1)^2+\frac12(X_n-1)^2=X_n^2+1$. The time $k$ has finite expectation (from any state the walk leaves $[0,100]$ within $100$ steps with probability $\ge2^{-100}$) and $M$ has bounded increments, so $E[M_k]=M_0=67^2$. At time $k$, $X_k\in\{0,100\}$ with $P(X_k=100)=\frac{67}{100}$, so $E[X_k^2]=100^2\cdot\frac{67}{100}=6700$. Thus $E[k]=E[X_k^2]-67^2=6700-4489=2211$ $(=67\cdot33)$.

**Answer: 2211**

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-17.title: Exponential martingale
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-17.body:
Let $r=\frac{1-h}h$. For $h\ne\frac12$, $r^{X_n}$ is a martingale: $E[r^{X_{n+1}}\mid X_n]=r^{X_n}\big(hr+(1-h)r^{-1}\big)=r^{X_n}\big((1-h)+h\big)=r^{X_n}$. It is bounded up to the stopping time (values between $1$ and $r^{100}$), so optional stopping gives $r^{67}=P\cdot r^{100}+(1-P)\cdot1$, hence
$$P=\frac{r^{67}-1}{r^{100}-1}=\frac{1-r^{67}}{1-r^{100}}.$$
For $h=\frac12$ the answer is $\frac{67}{100}$ (the limit $r\to1$). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-18.title: Find a harmonic function
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-18.body:
Positions are $\frac j{20}$, $j=0,\dots,20$; from $j$ go up with probability $p_j=\frac j{20}$, down with $1-p_j$; start at $j=12$. Let $h(j)$ be the probability of reaching $20$ before $0$: $h(j)=p_jh(j+1)+(1-p_j)h(j-1)$, so with $d_j=h(j+1)-h(j)$: $p_jd_j=(1-p_j)d_{j-1}$, i.e. $d_j=d_{j-1}\frac{20-j}{j}$, giving $d_j=d_0\binom{19}j$. Then $h(j)=d_0\sum_{i<j}\binom{19}i$ and $h(20)=1$ gives $d_0=2^{-19}$. So
$$h(12)=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{11}\binom{19}i}{2^{19}}=\frac{2^{18}+\binom{19}{10}+\binom{19}{11}}{2^{19}}=\frac{262144+92378+75582}{524288}=\frac{430104}{524288}=\frac{53763}{65536}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{53763}{65536}$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-21.title: Expand
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-21.body: $\mathrm{Var}(x+y)=E[x^2]+2E[xy]+E[y^2]-\big(E[x]+E[y]\big)^2=\big(E[x^2]-E[x]^2\big)+\big(E[y^2]-E[y]^2\big)+2\big(E[xy]-E[x]E[y]\big)$, and the last bracket is $0$ by independence. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-22.title: Additivity
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-22.body: By additivity of variance for independent variables, $\mathrm{Var}=n\cdot\frac{35}{12}=\frac{35n}{12}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-23.title: Direct
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-23.body: $E[\lambda X]=\lambda E[X]$ by linearity, so $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda X)=E[(\lambda X-\lambda E[X])^2]=\lambda^2E[(X-E[X])^2]=\lambda^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-24.title: Compute
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-24.body: Mean $=\frac{25}5=5$. Deviations: $-5,-2,-1,1,7$. Variance $=\frac{25+4+1+1+49}5=16$, $\sigma=4$. Distances in standard deviations $\frac{|x-5|}4$: $0\to\frac54$, $3\to\frac12$, $4\to\frac14$, $6\to\frac14$, $12\to\frac74$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-25.title: Markov-type bound
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-25.body: Let the data be $x_1,\dots,x_N$ with mean $\mu$ and let $m$ of them satisfy $|x_i-\mu|\ge n\sigma$. Then $\sigma^2=\frac1N\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\ge\frac1N\cdot m\cdot n^2\sigma^2$, so $\frac mN\le\frac1{n^2}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-26.title: Chebyshev with $n=2$
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-26.body: The sum has mean $1000\cdot\frac72=3500$ and variance $1000\cdot\frac{35}{12}=\frac{8750}3$, so $\sigma=\sqrt{8750/3}\approx54.0$. By Chebyshev with $n=2$ at most $\frac14$ of the sums are at least $2\sigma$ from the mean, so at least $75\%$ lie in $[3500-2\sigma,3500+2\sigma]\approx[3392,3608]$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-27.title: Recursion
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-27.body:
Let $E$ be the expected final amount. With probability $\frac12$ the first flip is a tail and you leave with $\$1$; with probability $\frac12$ it is a head and you effectively restart with $\$1.25$, whose expected final amount is $1.25E$. So $E=\frac12(1)+\frac12(1.25E)$, $E\left(1-\frac58\right)=\frac12$, $E=\frac43$ dollars. (Check: $E=\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j-1}1.25^j=\frac12\cdot\frac1{1-5/8}=\frac43$.)

**Answer: $\frac43$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-28.title: Explanation
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-28.body: The expected final amount is $E=\sum_{j\ge0}\left(\frac12\right)^{j+1}2^j=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac12=\infty$ (with $j$ heads the amount is $2^j$ with probability $2^{-j-1}$). The recursion $E=\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\cdot2E$ is only valid for a finite $E$; for $E=\infty$ the equation $\infty=\infty$ carries no contradiction, and subtracting $E$ from both sides is illegitimate. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-29.title: Explanation
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-29.body: With $j$ heads the final amount is $3^j$ with probability $2^{-j-1}$, so $E=\sum_j\frac12\left(\frac32\right)^j=\infty$ since $\frac32>1$. The recursion holds only when $E$ is finite; here it is meaningless (solving it formally gives the nonsensical value $-1$). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-30.title: Mean and variance
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-30.body:
The base-$3$ digits $d_i$ of a uniform real are independent and uniform on $\{0,1,2\}$ ($E[d]=1$, $\mathrm{Var}(d)=\frac23$). The base-$9$ value is $Y=\sum_{i\ge1}d_i9^{-i}$. Hence $E[Y]=\sum9^{-i}=\frac18$ and, by additivity of variance, $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\frac23\sum_i81^{-i}=\frac23\cdot\frac1{80}=\frac1{120}$. Therefore $E[Y^2]=\mathrm{Var}(Y)+E[Y]^2=\frac1{120}+\frac1{64}=\frac{8+15}{960}=\frac{23}{960}$.

**Answer: $\frac{23}{960}$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-1.title: Markov
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-1.body: By Markov's inequality for the nonnegative variable $e^{\lambda S_n}$: $P\big(e^{\lambda S_n}\ge a\big)\le\frac{E[e^{\lambda S_n}]}a$ with $a=e^{\lambda(\mu_n+t)}$. By independence $E[e^{\lambda S_n}]=E\big[\prod e^{\lambda X_i}\big]=\prod E[e^{\lambda X_i}]$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-2.title: Monotonicity
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-2.body: $\varphi(u)=\frac{e^u-1}u=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{u^{k-1}}{k!}$ has nonnegative coefficients, so it is increasing for $u>0$. Since $0<\lambda x\le\lambda$, $\varphi(\lambda x)\le\varphi(\lambda)$, i.e. $\frac{e^{\lambda x}-1}{\lambda x}\le\frac{e^\lambda-1}\lambda$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-3.title: AM–GM
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-3.body: The factors are positive. By AM–GM, $\prod_{i=1}^n a_i\le\left(\frac1n\sum a_i\right)^n$ with $a_i=1+E[X_i](e^\lambda-1)$, and $\frac1n\sum a_i=1+\frac{(e^\lambda-1)}n\sum E[X_i]=1+\frac{e^\lambda-1}n\mu_n$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-4.title: Comparison
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-4.body: For $0\le m<n$ and every real $x$: if $|x|\le1$ then $|x|^m\le1$, otherwise $|x|^m\le|x|^n$. So $|x|^m\le1+|x|^n$ and $E|x|^m\le1+E|x|^n<\infty$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-5.title: Binomial theorem
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-5.body: $(x-b)^n=\big((x-a)+(a-b)\big)^n=\sum_i\binom ni(x-a)^i(a-b)^{n-i}$; take expectations and use linearity (the factors $(a-b)^{n-i}$ are constants). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-6.title: Convolution
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-6.body:
Subtracting the means we may assume $\mu_1=\mu_2=0$. Let $s^2=\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2$. Completing the square in $x$:
$$\frac{x^2}{\sigma_1^2}+\frac{(z-x)^2}{\sigma_2^2}=\frac{s^2}{\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2}\Big(x-\frac{\sigma_1^2z}{s^2}\Big)^2+\frac{z^2}{s^2}.$$
Hence $f(z)=\frac1{2\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2}e^{-z^2/2s^2}\int e^{-\frac{s^2}{2\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2}(x-c)^2}dx=\frac1{2\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2}e^{-z^2/2s^2}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2}{s^2}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi s^2}}e^{-z^2/2s^2}$, the density of $N(0,s^2)$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-8.title: Direct
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-8.body: $E[Y_i]=\frac{E[X_i]-\mu}\sigma=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}(X_i)}{\sigma^2}=1$ (variance scales quadratically, shifts do not change it). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-9.title: (a) and (b)
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-9.body:
By independence $E[Y_1^{k_1}\cdots Y_n^{k_n}]=\prod E[Y_i^{k_i}]$ (with $E[Y^0]=1$).

(a) If some $k_i=1$ the factor $E[Y_i]=0$ kills the term, so these terms sum to $0$.

(b) Suppose no $k_i=1$ and some $k_i\ge3$. If $r$ of the $k_i$ are nonzero, then $k\ge2(r-1)+3$, so $r\le\frac{k-1}2$. The number of such tuples is at most $\binom nr\cdot(\text{number of compositions of }k)\le c_kn^{(k-1)/2}$ (for $n\ge1$), and each term is at most $\binom k{k_1,\dots}\prod E|Y|^{k_i}\le K_k$, a constant depending only on $k$ (all moments are finite). So the sum is at most $C_kn^{(k-1)/2}$ in absolute value, and multiplied by $n^{-k/2}$ it is $O(n^{-1/2})\to0$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-9.title: (c) and conclusion
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-9.body:
If all $k_i\in\{0,2\}$ then $k$ is even; for odd $k$ there are no such tuples (sum $0$). For $k=2j$ choose the $j$ positions with $k_i=2$: $\binom nj$ tuples, each with multinomial coefficient $\frac{k!}{2^j}$ and expectation $E[Y^2]^j=1$. Hence the sum is $n^{-j}\binom nj\frac{(2j)!}{2^j}\to\frac{(2j)!}{2^jj!}=(2j-1)!!=(k-1)!!$ as $n\to\infty$ (since $\binom nj\sim\frac{n^j}{j!}$).

Adding (a), (b), (c): $E[S_n^k]\to(k-1)!!$ for even $k$ and $\to0$ for odd $k$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-10.title: Moments of $G$
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-10.body:
Odd moments: $x^ke^{-x^2/2}$ is odd, so $E[G^k]=0$ ($\int|x|^ke^{-x^2/2}<\infty$). Even moments: for $k\ge2$, with $\varphi(x)=\frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ and $\varphi'=-x\varphi$,
$$E[G^k]=\int x^{k-1}\cdot x\varphi\,dx=\int x^{k-1}(-\varphi')dx=\Big[-x^{k-1}\varphi\Big]_{-\infty}^\infty+(k-1)\int x^{k-2}\varphi\,dx=(k-1)E[G^{k-2}],$$
and $E[G^0]=1$. So $E[G^{2j}]=(2j-1)(2j-3)\cdots1=(2j-1)!!$. These agree with the limits of $E[S_n^k]$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-11.title: Verify Carleman
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-11.body: The even moments of $N(0,1)$ are $\mu_{2i}=(2i-1)!!\le(2i)^i$ (each of the $i$ factors is $\le2i$). So $\mu_{2i}^{1/(2i)}\le\sqrt{2i}$ and $\sum_i\mu_{2i}^{-1/(2i)}\ge\sum_i\frac1{\sqrt{2i}}=\infty$. Carleman's condition holds, so the moment sequence $(\mu_k)$ determines the distribution. A distribution with the same moments therefore has the same cumulative distribution function as $N(0,1)$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-12.title: Independence
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-12.body: $M_{S_n}(t)=E\big[\prod_ie^{tY_i/\sqrt n}\big]=\prod_iE[e^{tY_i/\sqrt n}]=\big(E[e^{tY_1/\sqrt n}]\big)^n$ since the $Y_i$ are independent and identically distributed. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-13.title: Lagrange remainder
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-13.body: By the Lagrange form of Taylor's theorem about $0$ with $k=2$: $R(x)=\frac{e^z}{3!}x^3$ for some $z$ between $0$ and $x$; as $e^z\le e^{|x|}$, $|R(x)|\le\frac{e^{|x|}|x|^3}6$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-14.title: Expectation of the expansion
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-14.body: Take $x=\frac{tY_1}{\sqrt n}$ in $e^x=1+x+\frac{x^2}2+R(x)$ and use $E[Y_1]=0$, $E[Y_1^2]=1$: $E[e^{tY_1/\sqrt n}]=1+0+\frac{t^2}{2n}+E[R]$. By the previous bound, $|E[R]|\le\frac{|t|^3}{6n^{3/2}}E\big[e^{|t||Y_1|/\sqrt n}|Y_1|^3\big]\le\frac{|t|^3E[e^{|t||Y_1|}|Y_1|^3]}{6n^{3/2}}=\frac C{n^{3/2}}$ (using $n\ge1$). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-15.title: Logarithms
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-15.body: Put $u_n=\frac{t^2}{2n}+R_n\to0$, with $nu_n\to\frac{t^2}2$. For $|u|\le\frac12$, $|\ln(1+u)-u|\le u^2$. So $\big|n\ln(1+u_n)-nu_n\big|\le nu_n^2=O(\frac1n)\to0$. Hence $n\ln(1+u_n)\to\frac{t^2}2$ and $(1+u_n)^n\to e^{t^2/2}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-16.title: Taylor expansion
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-16.body: Write $f\big(T+\frac X{\sqrt n}\big)=f(T)+f'(T)\frac X{\sqrt n}+f''(T)\frac{X^2}{2n}+\frac{f'''(\xi)}{6}\frac{X^3}{n^{3/2}}$ with $T=T_{n-1}$, $X=X_n$. Taking expectations and using independence of $T$ and $X$: $E[f'(T)X]=E[f'(T)]E[X]=0$ and $E[f''(T)X^2]=E[f''(T)]E[X^2]=E[f''(T)]$. The last term is bounded by $\frac{CE|X|^3}{6n^{3/2}}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-18.title: Hybrid argument
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-18.body: Let $Z_j=\frac1{\sqrt n}(G_1+\dots+G_j+X_{j+1}+\dots+X_n)$, so $Z_0=S_n$, $Z_n=\sum G_i/\sqrt n$. Let $U_j$ be the sum of the other $n-1$ terms (common to $Z_{j-1}$ and $Z_j$): $Z_{j-1}=U_j+\frac{X_j}{\sqrt n}$, $Z_j=U_j+\frac{G_j}{\sqrt n}$, with $U_j$ independent of $X_j,G_j$. By the two expansions, the first two terms are identical (both $X_j$ and $G_j$ have mean $0$ and variance $1$), so $|E f(Z_{j-1})-E f(Z_j)|\le\frac{(E|X|^3+E|G|^3)C}{6n^{3/2}}$. Summing over $j=1,\dots,n$ and using $E|G|^3=\sqrt{8/\pi}$ gives the bound. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-19.title: Scaling and convolution
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-19.body: $\frac{G_i}{\sqrt n}\sim N(0,\frac1n)$ (variance scales by $\lambda^2=\frac1n$). By the convolution theorem for normal distributions (sum of independent normals adds means and variances), the sum of $n$ independent $N(0,\frac1n)$ variables is $N(0,n\cdot\frac1n)=N(0,1)$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-20a.title: Smoothness at the junctions
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-20a.body: On $(r-\epsilon,r+\epsilon)$, $f'(x)=\frac1{\epsilon N}g\big(\frac{x-r}\epsilon\big)$ with $g(t)=(t^2-1)^3$ and $N=\int_{-1}^1g\ne0$, a polynomial; so $f$ is smooth there. At $t=\pm1$, $g$ has a zero of order $3$: $g,g',g''$ all vanish at $\pm1$ ($g=(t^2-1)^3$, $g'=6t(t^2-1)^2$, $g''=6(t^2-1)(5t^2-1)$). Outside the interval $f$ is constant. Hence $f',f'',f'''$ exist and are continuous everywhere (all equal to $0$ at $x=r\pm\epsilon$ from both sides). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-21.title: Sandwich
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-21.body: $f_{p+\epsilon,\epsilon}$ is $0$ for $x\le p$ and $\le1$ elsewhere (and nondecreasing), so $f_{p+\epsilon,\epsilon}\le\mathrm{Ind}_p$; $f_{p-\epsilon,\epsilon}$ is $1$ for $x\ge p$ and $\ge0$, so $\mathrm{Ind}_p\le f_{p-\epsilon,\epsilon}$. Take expectations. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-22a.title: Comparison
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-22a.body: $f_{p+\epsilon,\epsilon}(x)=1$ for $x\ge p+2\epsilon$ and $\ge0$ otherwise, so $f_{p+\epsilon,\epsilon}\ge\mathrm{Ind}_{p+2\epsilon}$. $f_{p-\epsilon,\epsilon}(x)=0$ for $x\le p-2\epsilon$ and $\le1$, so $f_{p-\epsilon,\epsilon}\le\mathrm{Ind}_{p-2\epsilon}$. Since also $f_{p+\epsilon,\epsilon}\le f_{p-\epsilon,\epsilon}$, the claimed inclusion follows after taking expectations. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-22b.title: Density bound
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-22b.body: The difference is $P(p-2\epsilon\le G<p+2\epsilon)=\int_{p-2\epsilon}^{p+2\epsilon}\frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}dx\le4\epsilon\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ since the density is at most $\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-23.title: Minimize over $\epsilon$
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-23.body: Write the right-hand side as $a\epsilon+b\epsilon^{-3}$ with $a=\frac4{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ and $b=\frac{35(E|X|^3+\sqrt{8/\pi})}{32\sqrt n}$. For $\epsilon>0$ the minimum is at $a=3b\epsilon^{-4}$, i.e. $\epsilon=(3b/a)^{1/4}$, where the value is $a\epsilon+\frac{a\epsilon}3=\frac43a\epsilon=\frac43a\left(\frac{3b}a\right)^{1/4}=\frac43\,3^{1/4}a^{3/4}b^{1/4}$. Since $b\propto n^{-1/2}$, $b^{1/4}\propto n^{-1/8}$, so the right-hand side is always $\ge K n^{-1/8}$ with $K=\frac43\,3^{1/4}a^{3/4}\Big(\frac{35(E|X|^3+\sqrt{8/\pi})}{32}\Big)^{1/4}$, and the choice $\epsilon=c\,n^{-1/8}$ attains order $n^{-1/8}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-24.title: Via CLT
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-24.body: Let $Z_n=\frac{\sqrt n}\sigma(\bar X_n-\mu)$. Fix $M>0$. For $n$ large, $\varepsilon\sqrt n/\sigma\ge M$, so $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)=P\big(|Z_n|\ge\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}\sigma\big)\le P(|Z_n|\ge M)$. By the CLT, $P(|Z_n|\ge M)\to P(|G|\ge M)$ (the endpoints $\pm M$ are continuity points of the normal CDF), where $G\sim N(0,1)$. Hence $\limsup_nP(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le P(|G|\ge M)$ for every $M$, and letting $M\to\infty$ the limsup is $0$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-1.title: Disjoint blocks
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-1.body: Let $q=\prod_{i=0}^kP(X_0=s_i)>0$ and, for $j\ge0$, $A_j=\{X_{j(k+1)+i}=s_i\text{ for }i=0,\dots,k\}$. The $A_j$ depend on disjoint sets of the independent variables, so they are independent, and $P(A_j)=q$. Thus $\sum P(A_j)=\infty$, and by the second Borel–Cantelli lemma infinitely many $A_j$ occur almost surely; in particular, with probability $1$ the pattern occurs at some position $n$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-2.title: One base and digit
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-2.body: Let $x$ be uniform on $[0,1]$. Its base-$d$ digits are independent and uniform on $\{0,\dots,d-1\}$. Fix $a$ and let $\xi_i=\mathbf 1[\text{digit}_i=a]-\frac1d$ (independent, mean $0$, $|\xi_i|\le1$) and $T_n=\sum_{i\le n}\xi_i$. Then $E[T_n^4]=\sum E\xi_i^4+3\sum_{i\ne j}E\xi_i^2E\xi_j^2\le n+3n(n-1)\le3n^2$. By Markov's inequality, for $\varepsilon>0$: $P(|T_n|\ge\varepsilon n)\le\frac{E[T_n^4]}{\varepsilon^4n^4}\le\frac3{\varepsilon^4n^2}$, which is summable. By the first Borel–Cantelli lemma, almost surely $|T_n|<\varepsilon n$ for all large $n$. Taking $\varepsilon=\frac1m$ for all $m\in\mathbb N$: almost surely $\frac{T_n}n\to0$, i.e. the frequency of $a$ tends to $\frac1d$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-2.title: All bases at once
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-2.body: For each pair $(d,a)$ the exceptional set has probability $0$; there are countably many pairs, so the union of exceptional sets has probability $0$. Hence almost every $x\in[0,1]$ (in particular, at least one) is simply normal. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-3.title: Construction and weak law
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-3.body: For $n\ge2$ let $P(X_n=\pm n)=\frac1{2n\ln n}$ each (note $\frac1{n\ln n}\le1$) and $X_n=0$ otherwise; $X_1=0$. Then $E[X_n]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_n)=n^2\cdot\frac1{n\ln n}=\frac n{\ln n}$. By independence $\mathrm{Var}(Y_n)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{k=2}^n\frac k{\ln k}$. Split the sum: $\sum_{k\le\sqrt n}\frac k{\ln k}\le\frac n{\ln2}$, and for $\sqrt n<k\le n$, $\ln k>\frac12\ln n$ so $\sum\frac k{\ln k}\le\frac2{\ln n}\cdot n^2$. Thus $\mathrm{Var}(Y_n)\le\frac1{n\ln2}+\frac2{\ln n}\to0$, and by Chebyshev $P(|Y_n|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\mathrm{Var}(Y_n)}{\varepsilon^2}\to0$: the weak law holds.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-3.title: The strong law fails
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-3.body: Let $A_n=\{|X_n|=n\}$: independent, with $\sum P(A_n)=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac1{n\ln n}=\infty$. By the second Borel–Cantelli lemma, almost surely $|X_n|=n$ for infinitely many $n$. If $Y_n\to0$ held on an event of positive probability, then there $\frac{X_n}n=Y_n-\frac{n-1}nY_{n-1}\to0$, contradicting $\left|\frac{X_n}n\right|=1$ infinitely often (which happens almost surely). So $P(\lim Y_n=0)=0\ne1$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-4.title: Induction
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-4.body: $m=1$ is the definition. If it holds for $m$, then by the Markov property and total probability, $P(X_{m+1+n}=y\mid X_n=x)=\sum_zP(X_{m+n}=z\mid X_n=x)\,P(X_{m+n+1}=y\mid X_{m+n}=z)=\sum_zP^m(x,z)P(z,y)=P^{m+1}(x,y)$ (time homogeneity gives $P(X_{m+n+1}=y\mid X_{m+n}=z)=P(z,y)$). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-5.title: Paths
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-5.body: $P^m(x,y)=\sum_{z_1,\dots,z_{m-1}}P(x,z_1)P(z_1,z_2)\cdots P(z_{m-1},y)$ is a sum of nonnegative terms, so it is positive iff some term is positive iff there are states $x=z_0,z_1,\dots,z_m=y$ with all $P(z_{i-1},z_i)>0$, i.e. a directed path of length $m$ from $x$ to $y$ in the graph. Irreducible means such a path exists for every ordered pair, i.e. the graph is strongly connected. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-6.title: Return probabilities
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-6.body: Write $P_x$ for the chain started at $x$, $\rho_x=P_x(T_x<\infty)$ and $N_x=\#\{n\ge0:X_n=x\}$. By the Markov property at successive returns, $P_x(N_x\ge j+1)=\rho_x^j$. Hence $P_x(N_x=\infty)=1$ if $\rho_x=1$ and $=0$ if $\rho_x<1$, and $E_x[N_x]=\sum_{m\ge0}P^m(x,x)=\frac1{1-\rho_x}$, which is infinite iff $\rho_x=1$. So for each $x$: $\rho_x=1\iff\sum_mP^m(x,x)=\infty\iff P_x(X_n=x\text{ i.o.})=1$. $(\ast)$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-6.title: Transfer between states
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-6.body:
If $P^a(y,x)>0$, $P^b(x,y)>0$, then $P^{a+m+b}(y,y)\ge P^a(y,x)P^m(x,x)P^b(x,y)$, so $\sum_mP^m(x,x)=\infty$ implies $\sum_mP^m(y,y)=\infty$. By irreducibility this gives (4)$\Rightarrow$(5) (and (5)$\Rightarrow$(4) is trivial).

(5)$\Rightarrow$(3): all $\rho_y=1$. Start at $x_0$; each time the chain is at $x_0$ it reaches $x$ before returning to $x_0$ with probability $q>0$ (follow a shortest path), independently on different excursions, and $x_0$ is visited infinitely often, so $x$ is reached a.s.; then by $(\ast)$ and the strong Markov property it is visited infinitely often a.s.

(3)$\Rightarrow$(2) is trivial. (2)$\Rightarrow$(4): if $\sum_mP^m(x,x)<\infty$ then $\rho_x<1$ and $P_x(N_x=\infty)=0$, hence $P_{x_0}(N_x=\infty)=P_{x_0}(\text{hit }x)P_x(N_x=\infty)=0$, contradicting (2). So (2)$\Rightarrow$(4). Together: (2)$\Rightarrow$(4)$\Rightarrow$(5)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(2). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-7.title: Resets
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-7.body: At each step the chain jumps to $1$ with probability $\frac12$ independently of the past, so it visits $1$ infinitely often almost surely. Each time it is at $1$, the next $2025$ steps are all 'up' (reaching $2026$ at time $+2025$) with probability $2^{-2025}>0$, independently for different visits to $1$ (the corresponding windows of length $2025$ after distinct visits that are at least $2025$ steps apart are independent; or by the geometric argument: after each visit to $1$, with probability $\ge2^{-2025}$ the chain reaches $2026$ before returning to $1$). Hence the chain a.s. reaches $2026$ from $1$. Starting at $2026$, the first step goes to $2027$ or to $1$; in either case the chain returns to $1$ a.s. (it resets with probability $\frac12$ each step) and then reaches $2026$ again. So $P(T_{2026}<\infty)=1$: the chain is recurrent. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-8.title: Return probabilities
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-8.body: Each coordinate returns to $0$ at time $2m$ with probability $a_m=\binom{2m}m4^{-m}$ (and never at odd times), and coordinates are independent, so $P^{2m}(0,0)=a_m^d$ and $P^{2m+1}(0,0)=0$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-8.title: Estimating $a_m$
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-8.body: $a_m=\prod_{j=1}^m\frac{2j-1}{2j}$. Since $\frac{2j-1}{2j}\ge\frac{2j-2}{2j-1}$, $a_m^2\ge\frac14\prod_{j=2}^m\frac{2j-2}{2j}=\frac1{4m}$; and since $\frac{2j-1}{2j}\le\frac{2j}{2j+1}$, $a_m^2\le\prod_{j=1}^m\frac{2j-1}{2j}\cdot\frac{2j}{2j+1}=\frac1{2m+1}$. So $\frac1{2\sqrt m}\le a_m\le\frac1{\sqrt{2m+1}}$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-8.title: Conclusion
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-8.body: $d=1$: $\sum_ma_m\ge\sum\frac1{2\sqrt m}=\infty$. $d=2$: $\sum_ma_m^2\ge\sum\frac1{4m}=\infty$. $d\ge3$: $\sum_ma_m^d\le\sum_m(2m+1)^{-d/2}<\infty$ since $\frac d2>1$. By the criterion $\sum_mP^m(0,0)=\infty\iff$ recurrent, the walk is recurrent for $d=1,2$ and transient for $d\ge3$. ∎
